pairs.en: On the same day, the ninth of the month, we remember the holy apostle MATTHIAS.
*Judas went out — lifted up — on a noose;* *Matthias went in — lifted up — on the wood.* *About the ninth, the young Matthias was lifted up on the wood.*

He was one of the Seventy, and he was counted with the Eleven Apostles, in the place of Judas Iscariot — as it is written in the first chapter of the Acts of the Apostles. He preached the Gospel in outer Ethiopia — the country now called Chambesia — and after he had endured many punishments at the hands of the Ethiopians, he gave his spirit into the hands of God.

sections.heading: The Ten Martyrs of the Icon of the Saviour, and Maria the Patrician

pairs.en: On the same day we remember the holy ten martyrs who contended for the holy icon of our Saviour Jesus Christ — the one above the Chalke Gate: JULIAN, MARCIAN, JOHN, JAMES, ALEXIOS, DEMETRIOS, PHOTIOS, PETER, LEONTIOS, and MARIA the Patrician.
*Nine men, who had struck down the enemy of God,* *are made friends of God through their zeal.* *⟨…⟩, O Saviour, ⟨…⟩ —* *says Maria, like the myrrh of Mary.*

These saints lived in the time of the beast-named Leo the Isaurian, in the year 716. He hated the holy icons, and so he burned them in the fire. And because of this the patriarch of that time, the holy Germanos, endured many sorrows and hardships from the accursed Leo — for he had rebuked the emperor as impious and lawless.

Then the beast-named emperor tried to throw down the venerable icon of our Lord Jesus Christ, the one venerated above the Chalke Gate of Constantinople. The ladders were already being set up, and the long beams put in place, and the men were ready to cast the icon down. But athletes of Christ got there first. They seized one of the ladders, pulled it toward themselves, and so sent the soldier crashing down — the soldier who was pulling the icon down — and they killed him. But the impious emperor they cursed and anathematised.

When the emperor learned of it he burned with anger, and ordered that all who were found there be beheaded — and they were a great multitude, whose number only the Lord knows. These nine monks he ordered to be beaten with rods, then thrown into prison, and given five hundred strokes a day. So the blessed ones endured bravely, beaten for eight months. When the tyrant saw that they were worn out, he ordered that ⟨…⟩ be heated, and with them the faces of the martyrs to be burned; and at last they were beheaded at a place called the Kynegesion, together with the holy Maria the Patrician. He ordered their remains to be thrown into the sea. And so the immortal ones received the crowns of their contest.

(Nikodemos adds that it was not only men who seized the ladders and pulled down the soldier, but women also; and he points the reader to the holy Theodosia of Constantinople, who contended for this same icon of the Chalke Gate.)

sections.heading: The Holy Martyr Antoninus of Alexandria

pairs.en: The holy martyr ANTONINUS of Alexandria died by the sword.
*Antoninus's body lies in the dense ash,* *while his spirit takes on a strange brightness.*

This saint was an Alexandrian by birth. Seized by the governor of Alexandria, he was hung up and torn with hooks; and then, thrown into a burning furnace, he gave up his spirit into the hands of God, and from there received the incorruptible crown of martyrdom. His holy remains were found in the middle of the furnace, unharmed and whole, without the fire having harmed so much as a single hair of his head.

(Note that the Greek heading reads ξίφει — “by the sword” — and we have kept it here; but the entry itself, and the couplet with it, describe death in the fire. The two stand in the text as they are, in conflict, and we have not smoothed the difference over.)

sections.heading: Our Venerable Father Psoes of Egypt

pairs.en: Our venerable father PSOES of Egypt reposed in peace, at prayer.
*⟨…⟩ —* *⟨…⟩*
(Note that the verse couplet for Psoes could not be recovered from the damaged scan of the 1868 page, and his life could not be recovered either; rather than invent one, we leave the couplet open.)

sections.heading: The Finding of the Holy Icon of Christ Not-Made-by-Hands, at Camuliana

pairs.en: On the same day we keep the Finding of the venerable icon of our Lord Jesus Christ — the icon not made by human hands at Camuliana. The narration is given under the name of our holy father Gregory, bishop of Nyssa.
*How great then is the icon, ⟨…⟩ —* *it shows us the condescension of Christ ⟨…⟩.*

Our Lord Jesus Christ — righteous and holy, our God — is invisible in the essence of his divinity, unconquerable in his power, unchanging in his might. He is by nature the lover of mankind and the good one; the exact image of the Father; who was begotten of the Father before the ages, invisibly, and in these last days was born of a Mother and Virgin, without seed. This same Lord consented, once again, to be seen in a holy icon — out of his goodness and his measureless compassion. ⟨…⟩ There the Creator of all is seen by us Christians, bearing a character worthy of all reverence: there, in his coming in the flesh, born as a child; here, the same Lord consented, today, to be worshipped in an icon that saves. Once again the Master stooped down to his servants.

Come then, brothers and fathers, and listen. I want to tell all who fear the Lord what wonders took place at Camuliana, the new Bethlehem, and set them before your eyes. I, the humble Gregory, will tell of the precious and blessed woman Bassa, who was renamed Akylina — of the things that were revealed to me, the unworthy one, by the Holy Spirit.

This precious woman, Bassa — renamed Akylina — had a husband named Kamoulos, a barbarian, a pagan and an unbeliever, a moneylender of that place, in the days of the emperor Diocletian. But his wife Akylina, shown mercy by the divine grace, came to know the true God. She sought to live a devout life in secret, keeping the purity of her soul and body.

So the blessed Akylina did everything that the divine voice had told her; and — a dread and strange mystery — the Master Christ came down to her, he who is always and everywhere present, and never overlooks those who hope in him and cry out to him in their minds and love him with their whole heart. Together with the Lord came all the powers of heaven, at the fifth watch of the night (that is, in the last hours before dawn), singing the hymn of victory: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord of Sabaoth.” And that same Master who had once washed his disciples' feet and dried them with the towel — he himself then washed his holy face with the water in the vessel, with his immaculate hands. And having washed, he dried his immaculate and God-formed face with that clean cloth; and at once there was imprinted on the cloth the type and image of his divine-human form, his all-holy and most true character — as is shown to all, even to this day.

So as the Lord, in former time, by his love for mankind and his condescension, had shown his incarnation, so now he showed it to the precious and most devout Akylina. She, seeing these things brought to pass for her, gave great thanks to the Lord, and could not be sated with thanksgiving. She hid the holy character of the Lord in a corner of her house — for she feared her husband — and honoured it beyond measure. Foreknowing her falling-asleep, she made provision for this holy and not-made-by-hands and unpainted icon of the Saviour; and having written down the whole account of it, she placed that written account together with the holy icon, and sealed up the place.

After the blessed Akylina died, it was revealed by God to me, the unworthy Gregory, that at Camuliana, in the house of Akylina, in a certain place, the not-made-by-hands icon of the Lord lay hidden. So I went down to the place shown me, and I opened the wall, and I found a case, within which was the holy character of the Father's effulgence. And likewise I found the lamp still burning, which the holy Akylina had hung there over a hundred years before and more; and I found a small censer, which was still burning and giving the fragrance of incense. This I saw with my own eyes, I, the least of bishops; and therefore I made it known to all. And taking from there that not-made-by-hands and holy character of the Lord, I deposited it in the Metropolis of Caesarea. Through it many healings take place, as many as took place at the Lord's incarnation: the blind, the lame, the paralysed and the demon-possessed were healed at once — that the fullness of the grace and gift of the Holy Spirit might be shown, and that it might be known that the incarnate Word of the Beginningless Father, he himself, even now lives and is strengthened, and remains and reigns to the ages of ages.

These things happened at Camuliana. The hiding-away of the immaculate and not-made-by-hands icon of the Lord took place in the reign of the impious Diocletian, as we said above; but its manifestation took place in the reign of the pious Theodosius the Great, in the year 392, to the glory of the only-begotten Son of God and the Father.

(Note that Nikodemos himself adds: although the manuscript and the printed Synaxaristes attribute this narration to St Gregory of Nyssa, he searched the three published volumes of Gregory of Nyssa and could not find it; and even the style of the narration does not resemble that of St Gregory.)

The calendar of the Ecumenical Patriarchate commemorates on this day also Saint Constantine of Constantinople, Saint Euthymios of Rhodes, and Saint Herman of Alaska — whom Nikodemos does not carry in his Synaxarion of 1868.
Through the prayers of your Saints, Christ our God, have mercy on us.
